analysis.one_liner: Requires large online platforms and data brokers to tell users what their data is worth and let them delete it.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets the biggest data-driven companies — online services and data brokers with more than 100 million US users that make money from user data. It would require them to tell every user, at least four times a year, what kinds of data are collected, how that data is used beyond the service itself, and the dollar value the company places on that user's data, and to give users a single setting to delete it. The FTC would enforce those user-facing rules. Companies that issue stock would also have to disclose to investors, in SEC filings, the value of the user data they hold and the money they make selling or licensing it. The bill was introduced in October 2020, two months before the session ended, referred to two House committees, and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Users of the largest online platforms and data brokers, who would learn what data is collected about them, how it is monetized, and what the company thinks their data is worth, and could delete it with one setting. Investors would also get a clearer picture of how much of a platform's value rests on user data.

how_it_helps.text: Commercial data operators must, at least every 90 days, tell each user the types of data collected (including data collected by third parties under agreement) and how the data is used beyond the service the user signed up for [S2][S3].

Each user must be given an assessment of the economic value the company places on that user's data, and a way to delete that data through a single setting, with narrow exceptions for legal obligations, security, and fraud prevention [S3].

Companies that issue securities must disclose in annual and quarterly SEC filings the aggregate value of user data they hold, revenue from user data, and contracts over $10 million with third parties for collecting or licensing user data [S2][S3].
Violations of the user-facing requirements are enforced by the Federal Trade Commission as unfair or deceptive practices, with FTC penalties [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The large online platforms and data brokers covered by the bill, which would bear the cost of tracking, valuing, disclosing, and deleting user data on demand, and would face new public scrutiny of how much of their revenue comes from monetizing user data. Some of that cost could be passed on to users through advertising or service changes.

drawbacks.text: The bill only covers companies with more than 100 million US monthly users that earn material revenue from user data, so a large share of the data-broker and app economy would face no new obligations [S3].

Putting a dollar value on each user's data is genuinely hard; companies could report rough, gameable estimates, and the SEC itself was given three years to study the problem and had to develop valuation methods in consultation with standards bodies [S3].

Compliance costs fall on covered platforms, and companies that monetize data could respond by raising prices for advertisers, a cost that can reach consumers indirectly — an objection an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary users the bill offered real, concrete rights — knowing what is collected and being able to delete it — at a cost borne mostly by the handful of very large companies that profit from data. The main weaknesses are its narrow coverage and the difficulty of forcing companies to put honest dollar values on data, but those are design limits, not reasons the bill failed; it failed for lack of support and time.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with a single cosponsor, referred to two House committees, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Foster introduced the bill on October 2, 2020, with Rep. Seth Moulton as its only cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].

The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Financial Services Committee, the standard first step, and no further action of any kind appears in its history [S1][S5].
With the 116th Congress ending on January 3, 2021, roughly two months after introduction, the bill expired without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest online platforms and data brokers, which avoided new duties to disclose how they value and monetize user data, and to let users delete it. Investors also lost a proposed window into how much platform revenue rests on user data.

for.name: Rep. Bill Foster
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and took no recorded step beyond referral to advance it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never held a hearing or markup on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the securities-disclosure provisions and never considered the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; both sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican or opposition is on the record.

industries.industry: Large consumer online platforms (social media, search, large apps)
industries.note: Covered companies would have to tell users what data they collect, how it is used and what it is worth, and let them delete it, and would have to disclose user-data revenue in SEC filings. Their business depends on monetizing user data, so transparency and deletion rights cut directly against it.

Data brokers meeting the 100-million-user and revenue thresholds would face the same disclosure and deletion duties. Their revenue comes from selling information about ordinary people, so the bill's transparency rules work against their model.

Third-party contracts over $10 million for collecting, licensing, or sharing user data would have to be disclosed in SEC filings, and data-revenue would become visible to investors. Widespread deletion of user data could shrink the pool of targetable data the ad industry buys.
